passages.title: The Clock That Changed the World
passages.text:
In the early 18th century, the greatest scientific problem of the age was determining longitude at sea. Without a reliable method, ships were frequently lost, with disastrous consequences for trade and empire. In 1714, the British Parliament offered a prize of £20,000 – equivalent to several million pounds today – to anyone who could solve the problem.

The solution came from an unlikely source: John Harrison, a self-taught carpenter and clockmaker from Yorkshire. Over four decades, Harrison designed a series of five increasingly precise marine chronometers that could withstand the rocking, temperature changes, and humidity of ocean voyages. His fourth model, H4, was tested on a transatlantic voyage and lost only 5.1 seconds over 80 days, an accuracy far exceeding the requirements of the prize.

Harrison faced fierce opposition from the astronomical establishment, who believed the solution lay in mapping the stars rather than in mechanical clocks. The Board of Longitude, dominated by astronomers, repeatedly denied Harrison the full prize money, despite his clocks proving themselves in multiple trials. It took the personal intervention of King George III to finally secure recognition for Harrison's work.

Harrison’s chronometers revolutionised global navigation. For the first time, sailors could determine their longitude accurately, making sea travel safer and more efficient. This innovation facilitated the expansion of global trade routes, exploration, and colonialism in the 18th and 19th centuries. The principles he developed laid the foundation for modern timekeeping and precision engineering.

Today, Harrison’s original clocks are preserved at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London. They are considered among the most important technological artefacts of the modern era. His story, popularised in the book and television series 'Longitude', serves as a powerful reminder that world-changing innovations often come from unexpected places and that persistence in the face of established authority can ultimately triumph.

questions.q: 1. What was the major scientific challenge mentioned in the passage?
questions.justification: The text states that 'determining longitude at sea' was the greatest scientific problem of the age.

questions.q: 2. What was John Harrison's background before solving the navigation problem?
questions.justification: John Harrison is described as 'a self-taught carpenter and clockmaker from Yorkshire'.

questions.q: 3. How accurate was Harrison's fourth model, H4, during its transatlantic test?
options: Was less accurate than astronomical methods
questions.justification: The passage states that H4 'lost only 5.1 seconds over 80 days, an accuracy far exceeding the requirements'.

questions.q: 4. Why did Harrison face opposition from the astronomical establishment?
options: They wanted the solution to come from astronomy
Harrison refused to share his design
questions.justification: The text explains that astronomers 'believed the solution lay in mapping the stars rather than in mechanical clocks'.

questions.q: 5. How did Harrison finally receive recognition for his work?
questions.justification: The passage states that 'it took the personal intervention of King George III to finally secure recognition'.

questions.q: 6. What impact did Harrison's chronometers have on global trade?
options: They made sea travel safer and more efficient
questions.justification: The text explains that 'this innovation facilitated the expansion of global trade routes, exploration, and colonialism'.

questions.q: 7. Where are Harrison's original clocks preserved today?
questions.justification: The passage mentions 'the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London' where the clocks are kept.

passages.title: The Floating Forest of Bangladesh
passages.text:
During the monsoon season, the rivers of Bangladesh swell to become vast inland seas, submerging villages and farmlands for months. In response, local communities have developed an extraordinary agricultural system: floating gardens. These gardens are constructed by building rafts of water hyacinth, a fast-growing aquatic weed, which are then layered with compost and soil.

Farmers plant vegetables such as okra, bitter gourd, and spinach on these buoyant platforms, which rise and fall with the floodwaters. The system requires no chemical fertilisers, as the decomposing water hyacinth provides all the necessary nutrients. A single raft can produce crops for up to ten years, making it a remarkably sustainable method of agriculture.

Historically, this practice originated in the southern districts of Bangladesh, where flooding is most severe. Local knowledge, passed down through generations, has refined the technique over centuries. The floating gardens not only provide food security during the floods but also allow families to earn an income by selling surplus produce in local markets.

Recently, the Bangladeshi government, with support from the United Nations Development Programme, has begun promoting floating gardens as a climate-resilient solution for food security in low-lying countries. The practice, once dismissed as primitive by agricultural scientists, is now being studied worldwide as a model for adapting to climate change.

As sea levels rise and extreme weather events become more frequent, the floating gardens of Bangladesh offer a compelling example of human ingenuity in the face of environmental adversity. Researchers from countries as far as the Netherlands and Vietnam are now visiting Bangladesh to learn from these ancient techniques, hoping to apply similar principles to their own flood-prone regions.

questions.q: 8. What material forms the base of the floating gardens?
questions.justification: The text mentions 'rafts of water hyacinth, a fast-growing aquatic weed' as the base of the floating gardens.

questions.q: 9. Why don't the gardens need chemical fertilisers?
options: The decomposing water hyacinth provides nutrients
The floodwater is full of minerals
questions.justification: The passage explains that 'the decomposing water hyacinth provides all the necessary nutrients'.

questions.q: 10. How long can a single raft produce crops?
questions.justification: The text states that 'a single raft can produce crops for up to ten years'.
The passage says 'this practice originated in the southern districts of Bangladesh, where flooding is most severe'.

questions.q: 12. Which international organisation has supported promoting the floating gardens?
questions.justification: The text mentions 'the Bangladeshi government, with support from the United Nations Development Programme'.

questions.q: 13. Which countries are now visiting Bangladesh to learn from these techniques?
questions.justification: The passage states 'researchers from countries as far as the Netherlands and Vietnam are now visiting Bangladesh'.

grammarQuestions.q: I ___ my new job last month.
grammarQuestions.justification: 'last month' يدل على الماضي البسيط، والصيغة الصحيحة هي 'began' (بدأ).
'The people' جمع، لذا نستخدم 'are'.
نحتاج إلى ضمير ملكية (yours) يعود على 'umbrella' دون اسم بعده.
'big' صفة لا تجمع، و'cars' اسم جمع. الترتيب الصحيح: صفة + اسم.
'Thanks for everything' هو التعبير الشائع للشكر على كل شيء.
'parents' جمع، ولإضافة الملكية نضع الفاصلة بعد الجمع: parents' dog.
ظرف التكرار 'usually' يأتي قبل الفعل الرئيسي وبعد الفعل المساعد.

grammarQuestions.q: I'm Japanese. ___ family are from Tokyo.
grammarQuestions.justification: 'I'm' يناسبه ضمير الملكية 'My'.
للسؤال عن الماضي البسيط نستخدم 'Did + فاعل + مصدر'.
نفي 'can' يكون بـ 'can't' أو 'cannot'.
'We' فاعل جمع، والنفي يكون بـ 'aren't' (are not).
بعد 'like' يمكن استخدام المصدر أو الفعل + ing: 'like working'.
'We' فاعل جمع، لذا نستخدم 'haven't been'. خبرة حياتية (Present Perfect).
'work hard' تعني يعمل بجد. 'hardly work' تعني بالكاد يعمل.
للسؤال في المضارع البسيط مع 'you' نستخدم 'Do'.
'every day' مضارع بسيط، والفاعل 'He' مفرد، لذا 'reads'.
بعد 'didn't' نضع المصدر المجرد (book).
السؤال بـ 'Was Picasso' والإجابة المثبتة: 'Yes, he was'.

grammarQuestions.q: She ___ to the market every day.
grammarQuestions.justification: 'every day' مضارع بسيط، والفاعل 'She' مفرد، لذا 'goes'.
'British people' جمع، والفعل في المضارع البسيط يكون 'drink'.

grammarQuestions.q: There ___ telephone in my hotel room.
grammarQuestions.justification: 'telephone' مفرد، لذا نستخدم 'wasn't a' (لم يكن هناك هاتف).

grammarQuestions.q: Is Mount Everest ___ mountain in the world?
grammarQuestions.justification: للارتفاع نستخدم 'high' وليس 'tall'. صيغة التفضيل: 'the highest'.
نستخدم 'by credit card' للتعبير عن طريقة الدفع.
'another' + اسم مفرد تعني واحداً آخر (مشروباً آخر).
'never' ظرف تكرار يأتي قبل الفعل الرئيسي: 'never listen'.
للتعبير عن نية أو خطة مستقبلية: 'are you going to do'.

grammarQuestions.q: I ___ do my homework last night.
grammarQuestions.justification: 'last night' ماضي، لذا نستخدم ماضي can وهو 'could'، والنفي 'couldn't'.
'good' تُقارن بـ 'better than'. لا نستخدم 'more good' أو 'gooder'.
المضارع التام (haven't) يأتي بعده التصريف الثالث: 'seen'.

grammarQuestions.q: This is our new teacher. ___ name is Charles.
grammarQuestions.justification: 'teacher' مذكر (اسمه Charles)، لذا نستخدم 'His'.
'He is playing' هي صيغة المضارع المستمر الصحيحة.

grammarQuestions.q: I can't see. Where are my ___?
grammarQuestions.justification: عند عدم القدرة على الرؤية، نبحث عن 'glasses' (النظارات).
للسؤال عن الوقت نستخدم 'What's the time?' أو 'What time is it?'
'before' يدل على المضارع التام: 'Have you read'.
'have the bill' تعني نحصل على الفاتورة. تعبير شائع في المطاعم.
للتعبير عن الوقت: 'ten to nine' تعني العاشرة إلا عشر دقائق.
'would like' يأتي بعده المصدر مع to: 'to play'.

grammarQuestions.q: The elephant is ___ land animal in the world.
grammarQuestions.justification: 'big' صفة قصيرة، وصيغة التفضيل: 'the biggest'.

vocabularyQuestions.justification: The text describes Harrison as 'a self-taught carpenter and clockmaker'.
